kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer: Generic (no manufacturer branding on the ELEGOO-supplied board); documented here under Joy-IT's SensorKit X40 naming, since Joy-IT is one of the few brands to publish a formal datasheet for this common breakout
generic_equivalents: Other PS2/PSP-style thumbstick breakouts with 2 potentiometers + 1 switch
KY-023 clones sold under many brand names
identity.package: module (small square PCB, roughly 25mm x 25mm, with a tall plastic joystick handle on top and a 5-pin header)

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A thumbstick you can push in any direction, plus a hidden button when you press straight down, that tells the Arduino which way it's tilted.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Steering a robot, moving a cursor, or controlling motor speed and direction by hand.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Two small potentiometers (variable resistors), one for left-right and one for forward-back, are linked to the stick. Each forms a voltage divider: when the stick is centered, its output sits at about half the supply voltage; tilting it raises or lowers that voltage. Pressing the stick straight down closes a separate momentary switch that connects its pin to ground.

pinout.name: Button (SW)
pinout.notes: Connects to GND when the stick is pressed down; needs a pull-up (use Arduino's INPUT_PULLUP)

pinout.name: Y-position (VRy)
pinout.notes: Voltage from 0 to VCC depending on forward/back tilt

pinout.name: X-position (VRx)
pinout.notes: Voltage from 0 to VCC depending on left/right tilt

pins.pin_1_identification: With the header facing you and the joystick handle pointing up and away, the pins read left to right as Button, Y, X, +V, GND. Confirmed from the Joy-IT KY-023 datasheet's own pinout diagram, and matches the seed pin order.

electrical.operating_voltage: 3V to 5V DC (commonly run at 5V on the UNO)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: not published for this generic breakout in the sources checked
electrical.typical_current: roughly 0.5 mA per axis at 5V, calculated from the two 10 kOhm potentiometers acting as simple voltage dividers (5V / 10,000 ohm); not directly stated as a current figure in either source
electrical.logic_level: Analog outputs scale with VCC (0-5V at a 5V supply); the button output is a simple mechanical switch to GND and works at any logic level

key_specs.button_type: momentary, normally open, closes to GND when pressed
key_specs.center_output: about half of VCC on both axes at rest (about 2.5V at a 5V supply)

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Small square black PCB (about 25mm x 25mm) with a tall black plastic joystick cap sticking up from the center, and a 5-pin header along one edge.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Black PCB, black joystick cap; two small trimpot-style potentiometers are visible under the stick mechanism; silkscreen may read 'KY-023' on the back (ELEGOO-sourced units are sometimes unmarked).
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: 'KY-023' silkscreened on the PCB where present, plus pin labels near the header.
easily_confused_with: A plain potentiometer/trimpot module (no stick, just a knob)
a 4-direction D-pad button module (flat buttons instead of a stick)

example_connections.uno_pin: D3 (illustrative; any free digital pin works)

wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: None required; use analogRead() for X/Y and digitalRead() with INPUT_PULLUP for the button

handling_notes: Avoid yanking the plastic stick sideways with excessive force; the potentiometers underneath are small and can crack
Keep it away from dust/grit, which can make the potentiometers feel gritty or give jumpy readings over time
common_mistakes: Forgetting the button needs a pull-up (external resistor or the Arduino's built-in INPUT_PULLUP), otherwise it reads as floating or random
Swapping X and Y pins, which just mirrors the controls in software rather than causing damage

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Button always reads pressed or floats randomly
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: No pull-up resistor enabled on that pin
symptoms_and_causes.check: Set pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) in code, or wire an external pull-up to the SW pin

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: X or Y always reads 0 or 1023 no matter how it's moved
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: That axis pin isn't actually wired, or VCC/GND isn't connected
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure VRx or VRy to GND with a multimeter while moving the stick; it should sweep smoothly between about 0V and VCC

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Worn or dirty potentiometer, or mechanical damage
symptoms_and_causes.check: Check the centered voltage reading (should be close to half of VCC); replace the module if it stays off-center

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the module powered, measure VRx (or VRy) to GND while slowly moving the stick along that axis; the voltage should sweep smoothly from near 0V to near VCC and rest at about half of VCC when centered. Measure the SW pin to GND: it should read open (no continuity) at rest and closed (continuity) when the stick is pressed straight down.
